title: When Everyone Makes Sense and Nobody Learns
author: Daniel Willingham
summary: Daniel Willingham responds to the recent viral Nikole Hannah-Jones essay in The New York Times by asking why so much intellectual effort produced so little progress. He argues that every party behaved rationally: Hannah-Jones told a story that illustrates her causal model of parent pressure leading to better learning, the Times published a compelling first-person account, and commenters rushed to respond. The trouble is that a personal story cannot bear the weight of a causal model, and it supplies a fresh point of discussion rather than new evidence. Commenters therefore repeated familiar positions on choice, charters, integration and poverty. He defines a helpful outcome as some improvement in understanding that survives the occasion, and issues a friendly challenge to the commentariat to name one thing in each viral piece that sharpens their own argument.
points: A first-person story can illustrate a causal model but cannot test it, so the story itself cannot settle the debate.
Every actor in the cycle behaves rationally, which is why the pattern repeats without producing learning.
Viral articles create a strong reason to speak but not a comparable reason to rethink.
Willingham's proposed standard is that each commentator should identify one thing a viral piece taught them that improves or qualifies their argument.
quotes: Irked because there’s been an enormous amount of intellectual horsepower expended, yet the outcome has been so meager.

The story itself cannot bear the weight of this causal model. Hannah-Jones intervened and students didn’t learn more, but we can’t know whether the model is wrong or whether she simply didn’t intervene in the right way, with the right people, or measured the wrong outcome.

But the Times is not a scientific journal. It’s understood, especially in the context of a first-person story like Hannah-Jones’s, that we are getting her interpretation of events, not a mythic view-from-nowhere interpretation from social science.
They didn’t have anything new to say because a story is not new evidence which calls for new arguments. A story is a fresh point of discussion. The examples change, but the logic doesn’t.

Helpful would be “some improvement in our understanding that survives the occasion.” Someone’s mind would have to be changed, or at least, their predictions sharpened, their confidence qualified, or a disagreement clarified.
Too often, viral articles create a compelling reason to speak, without creating a comparably strong reason to rethink.
